items.readable_text:
Content:
A walk [MATH: w] of length [MATH: n] in a directed graph is a sequence of [MATH: n] edges [MATH: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n] with the associated vertices [MATH: v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1}] where each edge [MATH: e_i] starts at the vertex [MATH: v_i] and ends at [MATH: v_{i+1}] for [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n.] This can be written as follows:
[MATH: w=v_1 \overset{e_1}{\to} v_2 \overset{e_2}{\to} v_3 \overset{e_3}{\to} \cdots \overset{e_n}{\to} v_{n+1}]

Content:
In a walk, it is possible to visit any vertex or traverse any edge multiple times. As we can see, walks in a directed graph are defined exactly the same as in an undirected graph, except that traversal is only allowed along edge directions. For example, consider the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7f059990b901aee3701f1ecdb3d0bb65]

Content:
An example of a valid walk in this graph is as follows

Content:
[MATH: w_1=v_1 \overset{e_1}{\to} v_2 \overset{e_2}{\to} v_3 \overset{e_3}{\to} v_4 \overset{e_5}{\to} v_2]

Content:
Since this graph has no parallel edges, the walk above can be written just as correctly as follows:

Content:
[MATH: w_1=v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3 \to v_4 \to v_2]

Content:
Trails and paths in directed graphs are defined exactly as in undirected graphs:

Content:
- A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct.
- A path is a walk in which all vertices (and, as a result, all edges) are distinct.

Content:
Notice that the walk [MATH: w_1] above is a trail but not a path because it visits vertex [MATH: v_2] twice.

sections.normalized_html:
A walk of length [MATH: n] in a directed graph is a sequence of [MATH: n] edges [MATH: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n] with the associated vertices [MATH: v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1}] where the edge [MATH: e_i] is incident on vertices [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_{i+1}] (in this order) for each [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n.] This can be written as follows: [MATH: v_1 \overset{e_1}{\to} v_2 \overset{e_2}{\to} v_3 \overset{e_3}{\to} \cdots \overset{e_n}{\to} v_{n+1}] If the graph has no multiple (parallel) edges, we can drop the [MATH: e_i]'s in the above notation since any corresponding pair of incident vertices will uniquely determine any edge.

[MATH: v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3 \to \cdots \to v_{n+1}]

A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct.

A path is a walk in which all vertices (and, as a result, all edges) are distinct.

With that in mind, let's list all possible trails from [MATH: v_1] to [MATH: v_4{:}]

  • [MATH: v_1 \overset{e_1}{\to} v_2 \overset{e_5}{\to} v_4]

  • [MATH: v_1 \overset{e_4}{\to} v_3 \overset{e_3}{\to} v_4]

  • [MATH: v_1 \overset{e_4}{\to} v_3 \overset{e_2}{\to} v_2 \overset{e_5}{\to} v_4]

Therefore, there are [MATH: 3] distinct trails between the vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_4.]

The distance between vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] in a weighted directed graph, [MATH: d(u,v),] is the weight of the shortest path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] (i.e., the path with the least weight). If no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, the distance is considered [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
A walk [MATH: w] of length [MATH: n] in a directed graph is a sequence of [MATH: n] edges [MATH: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n] with the associated vertices [MATH: v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1}] where each edge [MATH: e_i] starts at the vertex [MATH: v_i] and ends at [MATH: v_{i+1}] for [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n.] This can be written as follows:
[MATH: w=v_1 \overset{e_1}{\to} v_2 \overset{e_2}{\to} v_3 \overset{e_3}{\to} \cdots \overset{e_n}{\to} v_{n+1}]

Content:
In a walk, it is possible to visit any vertex or traverse any edge multiple times. As we can see, walks in a directed graph are defined exactly the same as in an undirected graph, except that traversal is only allowed along edge directions. For example, consider the graph below.

Content:
Since this graph has no parallel edges, the walk above can be written just as correctly as follows:

Content:
[MATH: w_1=v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3 \to v_4 \to v_2]

Content:
Trails and paths in directed graphs are defined exactly as in undirected graphs:

Content:
- A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct.
- A path is a walk in which all vertices (and, as a result, all edges) are distinct.
